title: New cool starlet in our backyard
caption: The brown dwarf VVV BD001, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
celestial: VVV BD001 · constellation Ophiuchus · about 55 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO, and D. Minniti and J. C. Beamín (Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile).

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: At the very center of this VISTA image sits a newly discovered brown dwarf nicknamed VVV BD001. It lies about 55 light-years away, in the direction of our galaxy's densely packed center, and it was the first new brown dwarf found in the Sun's neighborhood by the VVV Survey.

Brown dwarfs are often called failed stars. They form the way stars do, but lack the mass to ignite hydrogen burning. They are larger than planets like Jupiter, yet smaller than stars. Being much cooler and dimmer, they are hard to find. Astronomers usually hunt them with infrared cameras and avoid crowded areas like the galactic center.

That makes VVV BD001 doubly odd. It is the first found toward the Milky Way's center, and it belongs to a class called unusually blue brown dwarfs. Why such objects are bluer than expected is still unclear. It turned up by chance during the survey.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (8.53 x 8.53 arcminutes) and distance (55 light years), the frame spans roughly 0.1 × 0.1 light-years. Its light set out about 55 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: VISTA observed this field in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
filters: 1.25 μm · Infrared J (Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy)
1.65 μm · Infrared H (Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy)
2.2 μm · Infrared Ks (Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy)
understand.eye: All three filters record near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and brown dwarfs are cool and give off very little visible light.

explore: VISTA, at ESO's Paranal Observatory, is described as the world's largest survey telescope. Its VVV survey aims to catalog a billion objects in the Milky Way's center, and its data have produced a 3D map of the bulge and an image of nearly nine billion pixels.
